representative_people.context: Wynter, Campbell, Chaney and Marks historicize changing explanations of mental illness while tracing the persistence of racialized assumptions. Version-of-record opening pp. 2–3 checked; attribution to this historical analysis, not clinical guidance or endorsement of historical racial categories. Selected programme passage pp. 2–3; clinicians are subjects of the 2025 study, not its coauthors. Their careers are not dated 2025.

baseline_node.label: Spatial history / Historical geography
baseline_node.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s · coverage through 2000
baseline_node.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.

Hoskins: The Making of the English Landscape (1955); J. B. Harley: “Deconstructing the Map” (1989); Doreen Massey: “Places and Their Pasts” (1995); Felix Driver: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Samuel; Raphael Samuel: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Driver; Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Paul Carter: The Road to Botany Bay (1987); Ian N. Gregory: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Southall; Humphrey Southall: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Gregory.

baseline_node.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. baseline_node.label: New social history
baseline_node.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
baseline_node.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996).

node.label: New social history
node.date_label: 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000 · proposed selected extension through 2007
node.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.
node.representative_figures_and_works: E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). A Crooked Line: From Cultural History to the History of Society (2005). The Future of Class in History: What’s Left of the Social? (2007).
